# Visual attention to and linguistic similarity scores of (in)consistent objects
```{r overall visual attention, include=FALSE}
#conduct the tests
t1 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted)
t2 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted)

t3 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 1],
            IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 0], 
            paired = T, alternative = "less")
t4 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 1],
            IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 0], 
            paired = T, alternative = "less")
```
The goal of this study was to explore whether linguistic consistency can be used as a proxy for visual consistency. Thus, as a first step, visual attention to the consistent object was compared with that to the inconsistent object. As can bee seen from Figure \@ref(fig:EyetrackingFig), viewers fixated more (`r apa_print(t3)$statistic`) and for longer durations (`r apa_print(t4)$statistic`) upon semantically inconsistent objects than on semantically consistent objects. These findings replicate the well-established semantic inconsistency effect on visual attention.\par
```{r eyetrackingdataplot preparation, echo=FALSE}
plotdata = as.data.frame(cbind(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted,
                               IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted,
                               IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency))

names(plotdata)[names(plotdata) == "V1"] <- "proportion"
names(plotdata)[names(plotdata) == "V2"] <- "duration"
names(plotdata)[names(plotdata) == "V3"] <- "consistency"

plotdata$consistency = as.factor(plotdata$consistency)
```

```{r Overall linguistic similarity, include=FALSE}
t1 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreOriginal)
t2 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory)
t3 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects)


t4 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreOriginal[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 1])
t5 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreOriginal[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 0])
t6 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreOriginal ~ IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency, 
            paired = TRUE, alternative = "less", mu = 0)

t7 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 1])
t8 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 0])
t9 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory ~ IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency,
            paired = TRUE, alternative = "less", mu = 0)

t10 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 1])
t11 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 0])
t12 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects ~ IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency, 
             paired = TRUE, alternative = "less", mu = 0)
```
Subsequently, we examined whether linguistic similarity can be used as a proxy for visual similarity. If so, one would expect lower linguistic similarity scores in visually inconsistent objects compared to visually consistent objects. To this end, the linguistic similarity of consistent object was compared with that of inconsistent objects. This was done using the scene-category label and the labels of all other objects in the scene, with only the scene-category label, and with only object-labels. The mean linguistic similarity between the (in)consistent objects and the scene category label as well as the other objects in the scene was `r apa_print(t1)$estimate`. The mean linguistic similarity between the (in)consistent objects and the scene category label was `r apa_print(t2)$estimate` The mean linguistic similarity between the (in)consistent objects and the other objects in the scene was `r apa_print(t3)$estimate`. One sided t-tests compared the linguistic similarity scores of the consistent and inconsistent objects. First, linguistic similarity to the scene category label and other objects in the scene was significantly higher for the consistent object (`r apa_print(t4)$estimate`) than for the inconsistent object (`r apa_print(t5)$estimate`, `r apa_print(t6)$statistic`). Second, linguistic similarity to the scene category label was significantly higher for the consistent object (`r apa_print(t7)$estimate`) than for the inconsistent object (`r apa_print(t8)$estimate`, `r apa_print(t9)$statistic`). Third, linguistic similarity to the other objects in the scene was significantly higher for the consistent object (`r apa_print(t10)$estimate`) than for the inconsistent object (`r apa_print(t11)$estimate`, `r apa_print(t12)$statistic`). This provides preliminary support linguistic similarity can capture the visual inconsistency effect.\par 
```{r tests 3 hypothesis 1, include=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
###linguistic similarity 
# --scene-category
t1 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 1])
t2 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 0])
t3 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 1],
            IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 0], 
            paired = TRUE)

# --object-category
t4 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 1])
t5 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 0])
t6 = t.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 1],
            IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects[IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$scene_consistency == 0], 
            paired = TRUE)
```
Finally, the differences between the consistent and inconsistent linguistic similarity scores was compared. This difference was computed based on the linguistic similarity of the (in)consistent object to the scene category-label and to the other object-labels. First, when using linguistic similarity to the scene-category label, the linguistic similarity to the consistent objects (`r apa_print(t1)$estimate`) was significantly higher than the linguistic similarity to the inconsistent objects (`r apa_print(t2)$estimate`, `r apa_print(t3)$statistic`; Figure \@ref(fig:LinguisticSimilarityFigure), left). Second, when using linguistic similarity to the other object-labels in the scene, the linguistic similarity to the consistent objects (`r apa_print(t4)$estimate`) was significantly higher than the linguistic similarity to the inconsistent objects (`r apa_print(t5)$estimate`, `r apa_print(t6)$statistic`; Figure \@ref(fig:LinguisticSimilarityFigure), right).\par

names(plotdata)[names(plotdata) == "V1"] <- "linguistic_consistency_score"

plotdata$category = as.factor(plotdata$category)

# Correlate linguistic semantic inconsistency scores with visual semantic inconsistency effect

```{r Correlations computation, include=FALSE}
#Scale the data
#IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted =
#  scale(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted)[ ,1]
#IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted =
#  scale(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted)[ ,1]

#Compute correlations
# --Scene category label and object label
cor_Fix_Ori = cor.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreOriginal,
                       IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted, 
                       "less")
cor_Dur_Ori = cor.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreOriginal,
                       IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted,
                       "less")

# --Scene category label
cor_Fix_Cat = cor.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory,
                       IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted,
                       "less")
cor_Dur_Cat = cor.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory,
                       IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted,
                       "less")

# --Object labels
cor_Fix_Obj = cor.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects,
                       IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted,
                       "less")
cor_Dur_Obj = cor.test(IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects,
                       IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted,
                       "less")
```
One sided t-tests were used to test whether the visual attention to the (in)consistent object correlated with the linguistic similarity score of the object. First, a one-sided t-test indicated that the overall similarity score was correlated negatively with fixation proportion (`r apa_print(cor_Fix_Ori)$estimate`, `r apa_print(cor_Fix_Ori)$statistic`; Figure \@ref(fig:LinguisticVisualConsistencyPlots), A) and fixation duration (`r apa_print(cor_Dur_Ori)$estimate`, `r apa_print(cor_Dur_Ori)$statistic`; Figure \@ref(fig:LinguisticVisualConsistencyPlots), B). Second, a one-sided t-test indicated that the overall similarity score was correlated negatively with fixation proportion (`r apa_print(cor_Fix_Cat)$estimate`, `r apa_print(cor_Fix_Cat)$statistic`; Figure \@ref(fig:LinguisticVisualConsistencyPlots), C) and fixation duration (`r apa_print(cor_Dur_Cat)$estimate`, `r apa_print(cor_Dur_Cat)$statistic`; Figure \@ref(fig:LinguisticVisualConsistencyPlots), D). Third, a one-sided t-test indicated that the object-category similarity score was correlated negatively with fixation proportion (`r apa_print(cor_Fix_Obj)$estimate`, `r apa_print(cor_Fix_Obj)$statistic`; Figure \@ref(fig:LinguisticVisualConsistencyPlots), E) and fixation duration (`r apa_print(cor_Dur_Obj)$estimate`, `r apa_print(cor_Dur_Obj)$statistic`; Figure \@ref(fig:LinguisticVisualConsistencyPlots), F). This supports our expectation that the magnitude of the semantic inconsistency effect that an object elicits correlates with the linguistic similarity of that object.\par

```{r Correlations analysis data preparation, include=FALSE}
#adjusted fixation number
FixProp_con = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted[seq(1, 44, 2)]
FixProp_inc = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted[seq(2, 44, 2)]

#adjusted fixation duration
FixDur_con = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted[seq(1, 44, 2)]
FixDur_inc = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted[seq(2, 44, 2)]

#overall linguistic similarity scores
LOriSim_con = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreOriginal[seq(1, 44, 2)]
LOriSim_inc = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreOriginal[seq(2, 44, 2)]

#linguistic category similarity scores 
LCatSim_con = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory[seq(1, 44, 2)]
LCatSim_inc = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory[seq(2, 44, 2)]

#linguistic object similarity scores 
LObjSim_con = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects[seq(1, 44, 2)]
LObjSim_inc = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects[seq(2, 44, 2)]

Lin_Sim_data = as.data.frame(cbind(FixProp_con, FixProp_inc, FixDur_con, FixDur_inc, 
                                   LCatSim_con, LCatSim_inc, LObjSim_con, LObjSim_inc, LOriSim_con, LOriSim_inc))
```

       FixProp_inc + LCatSim_inc,

       FixDur_inc + LCatSim_inc,

       Lin_Sim_data)
```
If linguistic similarity can be used as a proxy for visual similarity, consistent and inconsistent objects should lie on continuum. The correlations between visual and linguistic similarity should then be similar for scenes containing consistent and inconsistent objects. Indeed, a Fisher z-tests indicated that the correlations between fixation variables and linguistic similarity scores did not differ significantly between objects labelled as consistent and inconsistent.
First, a Fisher z-test indicated that the correlations between fixation proportion and linguistic similarity to the scene category-labels did not differ significantly between objects labelled as consistent and inconsistent (`r c3@pearson1898`; figure \@ref(fig:MergedConsistencyPlot), A). Second, a Fisher z-test indicated that the correlations between fixation duration and linguistic similarity to the scene category-labels did not differ significantly between objects labelled as consistent and inconsistent (`r c4@pearson1898`; figure \@ref(fig:MergedConsistencyPlot), C). Third, a Fisher z-test indicated that the correlations between fixation proportion and linguistic similarity to the other object-labels did not differ significantly between objects labelled as consistent and inconsistent (`r c3@pearson1898`; figure \@ref(fig:MergedConsistencyPlot), B). Fourth, a Fisher z-test indicated that the correlations between fixation duration and linguistic similarity to the other object-labels did not differ significantly between objects labelled as consistent and inconsistent (`r c4@pearson1898`; figure \@ref(fig:MergedConsistencyPlot), D). These findings support our hypothesis that semantically consistent and inconsistent objects can be placed on one continuum by using psycho linguistics as a proxy.\par
```{r MergedConsistencyPlot, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 18, fig.height = 10, fig.cap= "Scatterplots of the correlations"}
### Prop fixations
# --overall similarity
sp1 = ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity, 
             aes(x = semSim_scoreOriginal, y = proportionFixations_adjusted, color = scene_consistency), size = 2) +
  stat_smooth(data = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity, 
              aes(x = semSim_scoreOriginal, y = proportionFixations_adjusted),
              method = "loess") + 
  stat_smooth(data = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity, 
              aes(x = semSim_scoreOriginal, y = proportionFixations_adjusted, color = scene_consistency),
              method = "glm", se = F, alpha = 0.8) +

```{r Cat-obj correlations analysis data preparation, include=FALSE}
#adjusted fixation number
FixProp = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted

#adjusted fixation duration
FixDur = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted

#linguistic category similarity scores 
LCatSim = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory

#linguistic object similarity scores 
LObjSim = IA_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects

Lin_Sim_data = as.data.frame(cbind(FixProp, FixDur, LCatSim, LObjSim))
```
```{r Differences between correlations with the cat and obj scores, include=FALSE}
c1 = cocor(~FixProp + LCatSim|
       FixProp + LObjSim,
       alternative = "greater",
       Lin_Sim_data)

c2 = cocor(~FixDur + LCatSim|
       FixDur + LObjSim,
       alternative = "greater",
       Lin_Sim_data)
```
It was expected that the linguistic similarity of the (in)consistent object to the scene-category label predicts visual attention to the (in)consistent object better than the linguistic similarity of the (in)consistent object to the object labels of the remaining objects. First, a one-sided Fisher z-test indicated that the correlations between fixation proportion and linguistic similarity to the scene category-labels did not differ significantly between objects labelled as consistent and inconsistent (*z* = `r round(c1@pearson1898$statistic, 2)`, *p =* `r round(c1@pearson1898$p.value, 3)`). Second, a one-sided Fisher z-test indicated that the correlations between fixation proportion and linguistic similarity to the scene category-labels did not differ significantly between objects labelled as consistent and inconsistent (*z* = `r round(c2@pearson1898$statistic, 2)`, *p =* `r round(c2@pearson1898$p.value, 3)`).\newpage

# Quadtratic model
One interesting question is how object consistency values influence visual guidance. On the one hand, previous work established that viewers utilize neighboring objects as cues for exploring a scene further (see the introduction). This indicates that viewers direct attention to objects that are similar to the currently fixated one. On the other hand, previous work also established that inconsistent objects can draw attention. This indicates that viewers allocate attention to objects that are highly dissimilar to the currently fixated one. Operationalizing semantic inconsistencies as continuous places these findings on a continuum. On this view, semantic similarity guides visual attention in a parabolic way, forming an inverted U-shape. Objects with either low (i.e., semantically inconsistent objects) or high linguistic similarity scores will be fixated upon more frequently.\par
To test this possibility empirically, we compared the fit of a linear and a quadratic model when predicting visual attention based on linguistic similarity. We fit four models to test this possibility. The first two models predicted the adjusted fixation proportion on an object based on the linguistic similarity of that object to the rest of the scene. The latter two models predicted the adjusted fixation duration on an object based on the linguistic similarity of that object to the rest of the scene. The two linguistic similarity predictors were the linguistic similarity of the (in)consistent object to the scene category-label, and the linguistic similarity of the (in)consistent object to the remaining objects in the scene.\par
A square root transformation was applied to the adjusted proportion of fixations and to the adjusted fixation duration to address non-normality. Two models were fitted to the transformed data: a linear model and a quadratic model. The models were compared based on their goodness-of-fit statistics, including the adjusted R-squared, root mean square error (RMSE), and Akaike information criterion (AIC). AIC is a measure of model fit that penalizes for the number of parameters in the model. Lower AIC values indicate a better fit of the model to the data.\par

```{r Fixationproportion_linear_category_score, include=FALSE}
#generate linear model
Linsim_category = score = allObjects_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory
fix_sqrt <- sqrt(allObjects_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted)
linearModel <- lm(fix_sqrt ~ Linsim_category)

anova_linear = aov(linearModel)
aov_linearModel_sqrt = aov(linearModel)
radj_lin = summary(linearModel)$adj.r.squared
RMSE_lin = sqrt(mean(linearModel$residuals^2))

#generate quadratic model
Linsim_catgory2 = score2 <- Linsim_category^2
quadraticModel <- lm(fix_sqrt ~ Linsim_category + Linsim_catgory2)
radj_qua = summary(quadraticModel)$adj.r.squared
RMSE_qua = sqrt(mean(quadraticModel$residuals^2))
```
```{r Fixationproportion_comparison_category_score, include=FALSE}
anova_linear = aov(linearModel)
anova_quadratic = aov(quadraticModel)

# compare models
anova = anova(linearModel,quadraticModel)
```

## Fixation proportion
A linear and a quadratic model were fit to predict fixation proportion based on linguistic similarity to the scene category label. The quadratic model showed a significant effect of the quadratic predictor (`r apa_print(anova_quadratic)$statistic$polyscore_2`), indicating a significant deviation from linearity. Indeed, the quadratic model fit the data better than the linear model (*F(`r anova[2,3]`,`r anova[2,1]`*) =`r round(anova[2, 5], 2)`, *p* `r ifelse(anova[2,6]< 0.001, "< 0.001", paste0("= ", round(anova[2,6], 3)))`). The linear model had an adjusted R-squared value of `r apa_print(linearModel)$estimate$modelfit$r2_adj`, while the quadratic model had an adjusted R-squared of `r apa_print(quadraticModel)$estimate$modelfit$r2_adj`, indicating that both models had a comparable fit to the data. In line with this interpretation, the linear model had an RMSE value of `r round(RMSE_lin, 2)` and the quadratic model had a RMSE value of `r round(RMSE_qua, 2)`. However, the linear model had an AIC value of `r apa_print(linearModel)$estimate$modelfit$aic`, while the quadratic model had an AIC value of `r apa_print(quadraticModel)$estimate$modelfit$aic`, indicating that the quadratic model fits the data better. Figure \@ref(fig:ModelPlots) shows the scatter plot of the data with the fitted lines for both the linear and quadratic models. \par

```{r Fixationproportion_object_score, include=FALSE}
rm(linearModel, quadraticModel, anova)
#generate linear model
Linsim_objects = score = allObjects_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects
fix_prop_sqrt <- sqrt(allObjects_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$proportionFixations_adjusted)
linearModel <- lm(fix_prop_sqrt ~ Linsim_objects)

radj_lin = summary(linearModel)$adj.r.squared
RMSE_lin = sqrt(mean(linearModel$residuals^2))

# generate quadratic model
Linsim_objects2 = score2 <- score^2
quadraticModel <- lm(fix_prop_sqrt ~ Linsim_objects + Linsim_objects2)

radj_sq = summary(quadraticModel)$adj.r.squared
RMSE_sq = sqrt(mean(quadraticModel$residuals^2))
```
```{r Fixationproportion_plotprep_category_score, include=FALSE}

# create a sequence of values from the minimum to maximum score

# create a data frame with the predicted values from the quadratic model
quadraticPredictions2 <- data.frame(scoreValues, predict(quadraticModel, newdata = data.frame(score = scoreValues)))
```
```{r Fixationproportion_comparison_object_score, include=FALSE}

anova_quadratic = aov(quadraticModel)

# compare models
anova = anova(linearModel,quadraticModel)
```

scoreValues_sqrt_2 <- seq(0, .8, 0.05)
fixPredict_sqrt_2 <- predict(linearModel_sqrt,list(score_2=scoreValues_sqrt_2))
fixPredict2_sqrt_2 <- predict(quadraticModel_sqrt,list(score_2=scoreValues_sqrt_2,
                                                       score2=scoreValues_sqrt_2^2))


##### FIXATION DURATION ######
### do the same analyses with Category score ###
score_3 <- allObjects_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreCategory
fix_sqrt_3 <- sqrt(allObjects_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted)
score2 <- score_3^2

# linear model on square-root transformed data
linearModel_sqrt <- lm(fix_sqrt_3 ~ score_3)
quadraticModel_sqrt <- lm(fix_sqrt_3 ~ score_3 + score2)

scoreValues_sqrt_3 <- seq(0, .8, 0.05)
fixPredict_sqrt_3 <- predict(linearModel_sqrt,list(score_3=scoreValues_sqrt_3))
fixPredict2_sqrt_3 <- predict(quadraticModel_sqrt,list(score_3=scoreValues_sqrt_3,
                                                       score2=scoreValues_sqrt_3^2))


## object-object scores ##
score_4 <- allObjects_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$semSim_scoreObjects
fix_sqrt_4 <- sqrt(allObjects_fixationVariables_semanticSimilarity$fixationDuration_adjusted)
score2 <- score_4^2

# linear model on square-root transformed data
linearModel_sqrt <- lm(fix_sqrt_4 ~ score_4)
quadraticModel_sqrt <- lm(fix_sqrt_4 ~ score_4 + score2)

scoreValues_sqrt_4 <- seq(0, .5, 0.05)
fixPredict_sqrt_4 <- predict(linearModel_sqrt,list(score_4=scoreValues_sqrt_4))
fixPredict2_sqrt_4 <- predict(quadraticModel_sqrt,list(score_4=scoreValues_sqrt_4,
                                                       score2=scoreValues_sqrt_4^2))
# Create a data frame for each plot
df_1 <- data.frame(score = score_1, fix_sqrt = fix_sqrt_1)
df_2 <- data.frame(score = score_2, fix_sqrt = fix_sqrt_2)
df_3 <- data.frame(score = score_3, fix_sqrt = fix_sqrt_3)
df_4 <- data.frame(score = score_4, fix_sqrt = fix_sqrt_4)
